introduction-user-pools-vs-identity-pool.core: Cognito has two parts. User pools are a user directory and OIDC identity provider: sign-up, sign-in, MFA and federation with social or SAML IdPs, issuing JWTs (ID, access, refresh). Identity pools exchange identities (including user pool tokens) for temporary AWS credentials so apps can call AWS services directly.

first_principles.problem: Teams confuse the two and try to use identity pools for app login or user pool tokens to call S3.
truths: Authentication proves who a user is.
AWS API access needs IAM credentials.
derivation: **User pool** for authenticating users to your app/APIs.
Often **both**: user pool login → identity pool credentials.

analogy.title: A passport office versus a currency exchange
analogy.story: The passport proves identity; the exchange swaps it for local money (AWS credentials) to spend.
analogy.breaks: Currency exchanges don't limit what you buy; IAM roles strictly limit what credentials can do.

example.title: Mobile photo app
flow: User signs in via user pool → JWTs
App calls API Gateway with access token
Identity pool swaps ID token for S3 credentials

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Login and AWS access, each with the right tool.

the-authentication-flow-oidc-jwts.core: User pools implement OAuth 2.0/OIDC: after authentication the app receives an ID token (who the user is), an access token (scopes/groups for APIs) and a refresh token (to get new tokens). Tokens are signed JWTs verifiable with the pool's public JWKS. Use authorization code flow with PKCE for apps.

first_principles.problem: An API trusts tokens without verifying signatures or audiences, letting forged tokens in.
truths: Verification needs issuer, audience, expiry and signature.
derivation: Use **access tokens** for APIs, **ID tokens** for profile.

analogy.title: A signed letter of introduction
analogy.story: Anyone can read it, but only the signer's seal proves it's genuine and still valid.
analogy.breaks: Seals can't be refreshed; refresh tokens mint new letters without re-authenticating.

code.text:
import jwt
jwks = jwt.PyJWKClient(f'https://cognito-idp.{region}.amazonaws.com/{pool_id}/.well-known/jwks.json')
key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key
claims = jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256'], issuer=f'https://cognito-idp.{region}.amazonaws.com/{pool_id}', options={'verify_aud': False})
assert claims['token_use'] == 'access' and claims['client_id'] == CLIENT_ID

the-hosted-ui-authentication-out-of-the-.core: Cognito's managed login (hosted UI) provides ready-made sign-up, sign-in, MFA, password reset and social/SAML federation pages on a Cognito or custom domain, implementing OAuth flows correctly. You customise branding and redirect URLs, avoiding building and securing auth screens yourself.

first_principles.problem: A team spends weeks building login, MFA and password reset screens and gets security details wrong.
truths: OAuth flows are easy to misimplement.
derivation: Enable **managed login** with a **custom domain** (ACM cert).
Use a **custom UI** only if required.

analogy.title: Using a bank's official card reader instead of building your own
analogy.story: Secure, standard and maintained by the experts.
analogy.breaks: Card readers look identical; hosted UI branding is customisable within limits.

check.q: What must you configure on the app client for the hosted UI?
check.a: Allowed callback (redirect) and sign-out URLs, OAuth flows and scopes.

user-pool-configuration-the-key-settings.core: Key user pool settings: sign-in identifiers (username, email, phone), required attributes (mostly immutable after creation), password policy, MFA (TOTP, SMS, passkeys/WebAuthn), account recovery, advanced security (risk-based adaptive auth, compromised credential detection), app clients (with or without secrets, token lifetimes, auth flows) and email/SMS delivery via SES/SNS.

first_principles.problem: A pool is created with username sign-in and an immutable required attribute, and must be recreated to change it.
truths: Some settings can't change after creation.
derivation: Use **app clients without secrets** for SPAs/mobile.

analogy.title: Setting up a building's access system before tenants move in
analogy.story: Some choices, like the badge format, are hard to change later.
analogy.breaks: Buildings can rebadge over a weekend; user pools may need migrating users to a new pool.

example.title: Pool decisions
flow: Required: email only; custom attrs optional
SPA client without secret, access token 15 min

check.q: Why shouldn't a single-page app's Cognito client have a secret?
check.a: Browser code can't keep secrets confidential, so the client must be public (using PKCE).

triggers-the-logic-hooks-lambda.core: Lambda triggers customise the auth lifecycle: pre sign-up (validate or auto-confirm), post confirmation (create a profile record), pre authentication (block users), pre token generation (add claims, groups or scopes), custom message, user migration (lazy-migrate from a legacy system) and custom auth challenges. Triggers run synchronously, so keep them fast and reliable.

first_principles.problem: Users from a legacy database must move to Cognito without forcing password resets.
truths: Synchronous hooks add latency and failure risk.

analogy.title: Checkpoints along an airport journey
analogy.story: Extra checks or services can happen at check-in, security or boarding.
analogy.breaks: Airport checkpoints have staff on standby; slow triggers time out and fail sign-ins.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Users migrate on first login, keeping passwords.
